findings.description: Unchanged from round 1, now formally escalated rather than disputed or claimed fixed: tests/live/zombiemud.lua and tests/replay/zombiemud_session.jsonl are still built from a synthetic local mock server, not a real recorded session against zombiemud.org:3000, and no live run against the real server has ever succeeded. SPEC.md's M3 exit criteria still require 'one successful live run', and this exit command still has never been executed, let alone passed. I re-verified the Builder's ESCALATION.md is an accurate, non-fabricated record: (1) I independently re-attempted outbound TCP to zombiemud.org:3000 from this round's own environment, via both bash /dev/tcp and a fresh Python socket.create_connection call, and both timed out again, confirming the block is still in effect and not specific to any one environment instance; (2) this session's own environment.network documentation confirms the host is denied by policy and can only be added by a human via the environment's settings, which matches PROTOCOL.md's escalation trigger ('an action needs ... network access not already granted') exactly; (3) the escalation is not a disguised dispute -- HANDOFF.md explicitly agrees with round 1's verdict ('I agree with the Critic's call not to approve with this outstanding') rather than arguing the finding was wrong. Given all of that, I judge ESCALATE (not REQUEST_CHANGES, and not APPROVE) to be the correct verdict shape for this round: REQUEST_CHANGES would ask the Builder to do something it has already shown, twice now, that it cannot do from inside this environment, and APPROVE would let v0.1.0 be tagged and released (PROTOCOL.md step 6) without the milestone's own named live-server validation ever having happened, which is the same reason I rejected APPROVE-with-documented-finding in round 1. This finding stays open/deferred pending a human granting network access; it is not something further Builder rounds inside this environment can resolve, and it should not be read as blocking the rest of the milestone's work (see disputes_adjudicated and the M3-F2/F3/F4 dispositions below, all of which are otherwise resolved or acceptably scoped) -- only the tag/release step and final APPROVE remain gated on it.

findings.location: src/script_engine.cpp:26 (instruction_hook/InstructionBudgetGuard); Lua 5.4 lstate.c thread-creation path (lua_newthread, ~lines 290-302 of build/_deps/lua54-src/src/lstate.c)
findings.description: The instruction-count sandbox (SPEC.md section 4: 'Instruction-count hook ... aborts any single callback exceeding a configurable budget') can be bypassed by a wide margin -- not entirely escaped (round 1's hypothesis, re-tested and still correctly disproven for the single-coroutine case), but amplified far past the configured budget -- via repeated fresh coroutine creation inside one callback. Lua 5.4's hook state (hook/hookmask/hookcount/basehookcount) lives on `struct lua_State` (per-thread), not on the truly-shared `global_State` (verified by reading build/_deps/lua54-src/src/lstate.h directly: global_State's field list has no hook-related member at all). `lua_newthread` (the function behind `coroutine.create`) copies hookmask/hook/basehookcount from the *creating* thread at creation time and then calls `resethookcount()` on the new thread -- i.e. every freshly created coroutine gets its own full, independently-ticking instruction budget, decoupled from how much of the creating thread's own budget is already spent. A callback that repeatedly creates a short-lived coroutine, lets it do just-under-instruction_budget_ worth of real work, and discards it, pays only the cheap create()+resume() overhead against the *outer* thread's own budget each time -- so total real work executed inside one top-level callback invocation can be amplified by roughly the number of outer iterations, effectively defeating the 'aborts any single callback' guarantee for any script (malicious, or just written in an ordinary worker-coroutine idiom) that happens to spawn coroutines in a loop. This also means the Builder's round-2 explanation of *why* the round-1 hypothesis is safe (tests/critic/critic_lua_sandbox.cpp's updated comment, and the matching NOTES.md entry: 'lua_sethook ... installs the count hook on the whole shared global_State') is not just imprecise but factually wrong about the mechanism -- which is exactly how this related, still-live bypass was missed: the single-coroutine case happens to be safe (the hook is copied into the new coroutine's own state), but that same copy-and-reset-at-creation mechanism is what makes the amplification finding possible for the repeated-creation case.
findings.evidence: New adversarial test committed at tests/critic/critic_lua_coroutine_budget_amplification.cpp (added by this review, not yet wired into tests/CMakeLists.txt -- mirrors the round-1 precedent where the Critic added the test file only and the Builder wired it into the build in its next round). Verified locally (temporarily wired into the build, then reverted before committing, per that same precedent): a trigger callback that runs, per the committed test, `for outer = 1, 200 do local co = coroutine.create(function() ... for i = 1, 100000 do n = n + 1 end ... end); coroutine.resume(co) end` (200 outer iterations x 100,000 real loop iterations each = 20,000,000 total loop-body executions, several times instruction_budget_ = 10,000,000 once VM opcode overhead per iteration is counted) completes normally and echoes 'total:20000000' with NO 'instruction budget' error at all, in ~165ms. Confirmed against a fresh build of this exact commit (1d36d06), `cmake --preset release && cmake --build --preset release`, both with and without the test wired into tests/CMakeLists.txt. This is a real, reproducible bypass, not a theoretical one.
findings.spec_ref: docs/SPEC.md section 4, sandboxing ('Instruction-count hook ... aborts any single callback exceeding a configurable budget'); docs/agents/CRITIC.md 'Lua' guidance ('sandbox escapes ... instruction hook actually firing').

findings.location: src/main.cpp (is_valid_number/lua_id_or_label, and the M3-F4 client.reset_timer wiring); tests/ (no test file references main.cpp's handle_builtin at all)
findings.description: Neither of this round's two claimed fixes to main.cpp -- M3-F3's is_valid_number()/lua_id_or_label() injection-hygiene fix, nor M3-F4's #timer reset wiring to client.reset_timer() -- is exercised by any test. handle_builtin() and its helper functions are file-local to main.cpp (anonymous namespace, no header), and grepping the whole tests/ tree confirms no test file mentions handle_builtin, main.cpp, is_valid_number, lua_id_or_label, or reset_timer; tests/replay/zombiemud_session.jsonl + tests/live/zombiemud.lua (the one test that actually exercises the compiled mudclient binary end-to-end) never sends a '#' built-in command at all, only plain Lua via the test API. Per CRITIC.md's mutation-testing mandate ('for at least three components ... run the suite, and confirm a test fails. If none fails, that's a blocking test-coverage finding'), this is exactly that gap for a security-motivated fix: there is no automated way to notice a regression here (e.g. someone reverting is_valid_number's check, or reintroducing the pre-fix bare-splice bug) short of manual testing. I judge this major rather than blocking because the underlying M3-F3 injection is self-inflicted (interactive-user-only, as round 1 already noted) and both fixes are otherwise correct by inspection (verified in this round: every id/label/duration splice point in handle_builtin() is now covered by either is_valid_number() or lua_id_or_label(), and reset_timer's C++ binding mirrors the already-tested pause_timer/resume_timer/kill_timer pattern exactly) -- but a security fix landing with zero regression coverage, in a milestone whose theme is 'testing', is a real gap the Critic should not wave through.
findings.evidence: `grep -rln "handle_builtin\|main.cpp\|is_valid_number\|reset_timer" tests/` (excluding tests/critic/ and this review's own new file) returns nothing. Read src/main.cpp:151-224 (handle_builtin) end to end and confirmed AliasAdd/TriggerAdd (lua_quote on both args), AliasDel/TriggerDel/TimerAdd (is_valid_number-guarded), TimerPause/Resume/Reset/Kill (lua_id_or_label) cover every splice point; only BuiltinCommand::Lua splices cmd.raw_args unescaped, which is the intentional, by-design '#lua <code>' passthrough, not a gap.
findings.spec_ref: docs/agents/CRITIC.md 'Adversarial tests' / 'Mutation check' (test-coverage requirement for anything security- or correctness-relevant that changed this round).

disputes_adjudicated.reason: Not disputed by the Builder (escalated, and explicitly agreed with round 1's verdict); I independently re-confirmed the same network block this round and judge escalation the correct handling, not resolution -- see the M3-F1 finding above for why this keeps the verdict from being APPROVE.

Resolved. Re-read .github/workflows/release.yml lines 61-67: the 'Configure' step now sets `shell: bash` explicitly (rather than relying on the platform default, which is pwsh on windows-2022) and passes the tag-derived version through `env: MUDCLIENT_VERSION: ${{ steps.version.outputs.version }}`, reading it back as `"$MUDCLIENT_VERSION"` in the `run:` block -- never spliced into `${{ }}`-templated shell text. Forcing `shell: bash` on both matrix legs (rather than leaving Windows on its OS default) is exactly what closes the 'works identically on the Windows leg' gap I asked round 2 to check: both legs now use the same shell and the same env-var-based quoting, so there's no platform-specific reintroduction of the original vulnerability. Verified by direct inspection; CI for this exact commit (1d36d06) is green on all 4 matrix jobs including windows-msvc (workflow run 36228824583), though release.yml itself has still never executed end to end (only runs on a version-tag push), consistent with HANDOFF.md's own statement and not something achievable before v0.1.0 is tagged.

The specific injection gap named in round 1 is closed for every call site (see M3-NEW-2's evidence for the full enumeration), including a real latent bug the Builder incidentally caught (a bare numeric timer id at the prompt was previously always looked up as a string label). Not fully resolved as a milestone concern, however -- see M3-NEW-2 (major, new this round): the fix itself has zero test coverage, which is a real, if narrower, gap of its own that I'm not willing to silently let ride under 'M3-F3: fixed.'

#timer reset is genuinely fixed: client.reset_timer() is wired identically to the already-tested pause_timer/resume_timer/kill_timer pattern (asio::post onto network_io_, TimerManager::reset(id) which already existed pre-M3), verified by direct reading of src/script_engine.cpp. #timer list remaining a placeholder is an acceptable partial resolution for what round 1 rated a minor, self-disclosed, already-untested finding -- TimerManager has no enumeration API to draw on, adding one is a real (if small) scope expansion beyond what a 'minor' finding warrants forcing in this round, and the Builder flagged it again rather than silently re-closing it. I'm marking the finding itself not-upheld (the fix for the part that mattered, #timer reset, is real and correct) rather than reopening M3-F4 outright, but noting -- as M3-NEW-2 also covers -- that reset_timer's wiring is untested.
